parameters.description: Specify the [OCIO|/solaris/ocio] color output space for the component. === Filters === (filters)

parameters.label: Denoiser
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: Choose a denoiser to run on the finished image output, or __No Denoiser__. This utility currently supports [Intel Open Image Denoise|https://openimagedenoise.github.io] (included with Houdini) and the [NVIDIA OptiX Denoiser|https://developer.nvidia.com/optix-denoiser] (must be installed separately). You must be on a supported platform and have the chosen denoising library installed for this to work.

parameters.label: Use Albedo
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: Some denoising libraries can use albedo to get a better sense of the image, guiding how and where it reduces noise.

parameters.label: Use N Input
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: Some denoising libraries can use normals to get a better sense of the image, guiding how and where it reduces noise. <!---

parameters.label: AOVS
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: Space-separated list of AOVs to run the denoiser on.

parameters.label: Tone Map
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: The basic idea behind tone mapping is the conversion from HDR real world luminances to LDR display values, i.e. for making images displayable on monitors. Another aspect is to simulate a particular film look. Film material is designed to have a certain "response" to light to enhance contrast and colors, represented as a characteristic curve. A filmic tone mapping curve is subdivided into toe, shoulder and linear sections for an image's dark, bright, and mid tones. Houdini provides several common operators for filmic tone mapping and each operator applies a specific S-shaped tone mapping curve. * __Reinhard__, __Ward__ and __Aces__ don't provide any further parameters to adjust the toe, shoulder and linear sections. * __Hable__, __Hable2__ and __Unreal__, however, have specific parameters for customizing the curve.

parameters.label: Tonemap Curve
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: Tone map curves apply to the __Reinhard__, __Unreal__, __Aces__ and __Hable__ operators. The curve is a visual representation of the mathematical model of each operator. You can fine-tune tone mapping through the curve's control points.

parameters.label: AOVs
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: Space-separated list of AOVs that will be affected by the chosen __Tone Map__ operator.

parameters.label: Toe
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: This parameter applies to the __Hable__, __Hable2__ and __Unreal__ operators and ranges between `0` and `1`. The default values for __Hable__ and __Hable2__ is `0.5`. For __Unreal__, the default value is `0.55`. The value controls the strength (curvature) of the toe segment in dark areas. Higher values create a darker image, smaller values brighten the dark tones.

parameters.label: Shoulder
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: This parameter applies to the __Hable__, __Hable2__ and __Unreal__ operators and ranges between `0`and `1`. The default values for __Hable__ and __Hable2__ is `0.5`. For __Unreal__, the default value is `0.26`. __Shoulder__ controls to curve's amount of curvature for bright tone values. The value affects where the shoulder curve starts in the graph: a value of `1` means that the shoulder starts exactly where the toe ends.

parameters.label: Slope
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: This parameter applies to the __Unreal__ operator and ranges between `0` and `1`. The default value is `0.88`. Controls the tone mapping curve's steepness, where higher settings (steeper curve) make the image darker and increase contrast; smaller values brighten the image and make it pale.

parameters.label: Linear
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: This parameter applies to the __Hable__ operator and ranges between `0` and `2`. The default value is `0.3`. Tones in the linear section should not (or hardly) change during the tone mapping process and represent the image's original tones. The __Linear__ value describes the distance between toe and shoulder. Higher values mean that the tow and shoulder sections become smaller, while more tones remain unchanged: the overall curve becomes more linear.

parameters.label: Linear Angle
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: This parameter applies to the __Hable__ operator and ranges between `0` and `1`. The default value is `0.1`. Here you control the slope of the linear part of the tone mapping curve.

parameters.label: Toe Length
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: This parameter applies to the __Hable2__ operator and ranges between `0` and `1`.  The default value is `0.5`. A small value creates a short toe section that quickly transitions into the linear section. A value of `0` eliminates the toe, and value of `1` means the toe takes up half the curve. Note that there are two ways to disable the toe: you can either set __Toe Length__ or __Toe__ to `0`.

parameters.label: Shoulder Length
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: This parameter applies to the __Hable2__ operator and ranges between `0` and `1`.  The default value is `0.5`. __Shoulder Length__ describes how many F stops you want to add to the dynamic range of the curve. Here you control the transition point from the linear section to the shoulder section.

parameters.label: Shoulder Angle
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: This parameter applies to the __Hable2__ operator and ranges between `0` and `1`.  The default value is `1`. Here you control how much overshoot you want to add the curve's shoulder.

parameters.label: OCIO
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: [OCIO|/solaris/ocio] image filters can be added to various render vars/image planes.

parameters.label: Enable
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: Enables the OCIO image filter defined below.

parameters.label: Planes
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: The render var names to which the OCIO image filter will be applied.

parameters.label: Output Space
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: Specify the OCIO color output space the image filter will apply.

parameters.label: Input Space
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: In most cases this should be left at `data`. There may be some strange case where the source of the AOV is already in a defined color space, in which case you can specify the source space here.

parameters.label: Looks
parameters.heading: Image Filters
parameters.description: Space-separated list of looks to apply to the finished image. A "look" is a named OCIO color transform, usually intended to achieve an artistic effect. See the OCIO documentation for more information.

parameters.label: Color Limits
parameters.heading: Sample Filters
parameters.description: A color limit clamps the value a shading sample is allowed to contribute to an LPE image plane, to reduce appearance of "fireflies" caused by undersampling of extremely bright light sources. This multiparm lets you apply separate limits to different sets of render vars.

parameters.label: Enable
parameters.heading: Sample Filters
parameters.description: Enables the color limit sample filter defined below.

parameters.label: Planes
parameters.heading: Sample Filters
parameters.description: A space-separated list of AOV names to which this color limit will be applied.

parameters.label: Limit
parameters.heading: Sample Filters
parameters.description: The maximum value a shading sample is allowed to contribute to these AOVs.

parameters.label: Aspect Ratio Conform Policy
parameters.heading: Aspect Ratio
parameters.description: What to do if the aspect ratio of the output image (__Resolution__ width divided by height) doesn't match the aspect ratio of the camera aperture (controlled by attributes on the camera). This allows a standard renderer to do something reasonable when you switch between cameras.

parameters.label: Data Window NDC
parameters.heading: Aspect Ratio
parameters.description: Directs the renderer to only render within this window of the entire output image. You specify the window as `minX, minY, maxX, maxY`, where each number is a normalized value from `0` to `1`. `0, 0` is the bottom left, `1, 1` is the top right, `0.5, 0.5` is the center, and so on. The default is `0, 0, 1, 1` (no cropping). Note that you can use _negative_ values. For example, `-0.1, -0.1, 1.1, 1.1` will give you 10% overscan on each side. There's also an associated dropdown menu with several preadjusted percentage values. You can use this window to temporarily _crop_ the render to a smaller region, for testing purposes. Pixels are only rendered if they are _fully_ inside the window. The normalized coordinates map to the image _after_ any adjustments by the __Aspect ratio conform policy__.

parameters.label: Pixel Aspect Ratio
parameters.heading: Aspect Ratio
parameters.description: The aspect ratio (width/height) of image _pixels_ (_not_ the image itself). The default is `1.0`, indicating square pixels.

parameters.label: Deep Camera Map
parameters.heading: Meta Data
parameters.description: Generate a deep camera map image recording depth. Deep camera maps are rendered images, where semi-transparent areas (such as volumes) between the camera and the nearest opaque surface are stored with depth information. Each pixel in the image is represented as a curve describing how the transparency value changes across the depth of the scene. This allows you to composite rendered images and have the semi-transparent areas blend correctly according to their depth.

parameters.label: DCM Filename
parameters.heading: Meta Data
parameters.description: The filename to save the deep camera map image to (this should be an `.exr` file). Include `$F` in the file name to insert the frame number. This is necessary when rendering animation. See [expressions in file names|/render/expressions] for more information.

parameters.label: DCM Render Vars
parameters.heading: Meta Data
parameters.description: Space separated list of RenderVar _prim paths_ (_not_ a list of AOV names). These must be the fully qualified path to the RenderVar prim and the render var name. You can use patterns to match multiple prims. The default is `/Render/Products/Vars/*`, which matches all prims in the branch where Houdini usually creates RenderVar prims. You can also leave this field empty to omit all RenderVars and only include alpha and depth planes (like a Deep Shadow Map).

parameters.label: DCM Z-Bias
parameters.heading: Meta Data
parameters.description: == Advanced == (advanced_tab)

parameters.label: Pixel Oracle
parameters.heading: Primary Samples
parameters.description: When rendering, a Pixel Oracle tells karma which pixels need additional sampling and which pixels are converged. This parameter tells karma which oracle to use.

parameters.label: Minimum Samples
parameters.heading: Primary Samples
parameters.description: The minimum number of camera rays (primary samples) for each pixel.

parameters.label: Plane
parameters.heading: Primary Samples
parameters.description: The AOV to use to measure variance.

parameters.label: Variance Threshold
parameters.heading: Primary Samples
parameters.description: The amount of variance that triggers more rays.

parameters.label: Random Seed
parameters.heading: Primary Samples
parameters.description: Variance sampling involves some randomness. You can change this number to get slightly different results.

parameters.label: OCIO Transform
parameters.heading: Primary Samples
parameters.description: Whether to apply an OCIO transform to the pixels before measuring variance.

parameters.label: Noise Level
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: Noise threshold to determine the number of indirect rays cast for indirect bounce when the __Convergence Mode__ is set to __Automatic__. Decreasing this threshold (for example, to `0.001`) will theoretically send more indirect rays and decrease noise, however the "extra" rays will likely be cancelled out by the __Max Ray Samples__ parameter. The correct way to decrease noise is to increase the number of samples per pixel, rather than change this threshold. If you are using __Variance Pixel Oracle__, you should set the same value for both threshold parameters. Setting the oracle's threshold lower may make the indirect component reach its threshold sooner and cast fewer indirect rays, but the oracle decides to cast more expensive camera rays because the amount of final noise in the beauty pass is higher than the oracle's threshold.

parameters.label: Enable Indirect Guiding
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: When turned on, Karma does a pre-render to roughly estimate of the light in the scene, and uses that to guide indirect diffuse rays, rather than just relying on the BSDF sampling distribution. This can improve "difficult" lighting (for example, caustics, and mostly indirect lighting), but can make "easy" lighting noisier. Before using this, you can try rendering direct and indirect AOVs to see where the noise is. If the noise is mostly caused by the direct lighting, there's no point in turning on path guiding. <!---

parameters.label: Display
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: When __OCIO Transform__ is __Display View__, the display to transform to before measuring variance.

parameters.label: View
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: When __OCIO Transform__ is __Display View__, the view to transform to before measuring variance.

parameters.label: Color Space
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: When __OCIO Transform__ is __Explicit__, the color space to transform to before measuring variance. ---> === Checkpointing === (checkpointing_tab)

parameters.label: Output Checkpoint Files
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: When this is on, Karma will periodically write out image tile data to a checkpoint file.  If the process is terminated before completing the render, you can resume it by turning on __Resume from Checkpoint__ and restarting.

parameters.label: Checkpoint File
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: When __Output checkpoint files__ is on, the name of the checkpoint file to write to. The default (`$HIP/render/$HIPNAME.$OS.$F4.checkpoint`) puts the checkpoint file inside a `render` directory next to the current scene file, and includes the base name of the current scene file (`$HIPNAME`), this node's name (`$OS`), and the render frame (`$F`) in the filename to help avoid two processes trying to use the same checkpoint file at the same time.

parameters.label: Save Frequency
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: When __Output checkpoint files__ is on, Karma waits this number of seconds between writing out a checkpoint file. The default is `60`.

parameters.label: Resume From Checkpoint
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: If this is on and you start a render and the renderer notices there is a valid checkpoint file, it will try to resume rendering from that checkpoint. If you want to restart the render from the beginning, you can turn this off or just delete the checkpoint file(s). === Buckets and Caching === (tiles_and_caching_tab)

parameters.label: Image Mode
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: Determines how the image will be rendered.

parameters.label: Progressive Passes
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: When rendering in bucket mode (see `imagemode`), this is the number of progressive passes over the image to perform before switching to bucket mode.

parameters.label: Bucket Size
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: Karma breaks down an image into multiple buckets for rendering. This is the side length (in pixels) of the square bucket. The default is 32, specifying a 32 pixel x 32 pixel bucket. Threads operate at the bucket level, so it might be useful to lower the bucket size if there are only a few buckets that are particularly expensive. That way the expensive areas can be divided across more threads. For example, if the image is mostly empty, but there's a distant object that fits within single 32 x 32 bucket, then that object will only be rendered using 1 thread. If you switch to a 16 x 16 bucket, then the object might be split across 4 buckets and have 4 threads working on it. Ideally changing the bucket size doesn't change the results, but Karma measures variance across pixels within the current bucket, so if you set it to a low value, for example 4, Karma only has `4 x 4 = 16` pixels to look at, so Karma will tend to make very poor variance estimates. This can show up as black pixels, where pixel rendering terminated prematurely due to a bad variance estimate.

parameters.label: Cache Limit
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: Whether to use a fixed size cache (`karma:global:cachesize`) or whether to use a proportion of physical memory (`karma:global:cacheratio`).

parameters.label: Cache Memory Ratio
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: The proportion of physical memory Karma will use for its unified cache. For example, with the default `vm_cacheratio` of `0.25` and 16 Gb of physical memory, Karma will use 4 Gb for its unified cache. The unified cache stores dynamic, unloadable data used by the render

parameters.label: Cancel Render if Missing Texture is Discovered
parameters.label_norm: cancel render if missing texture is discovered
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: Turning on this option will cause Karma to stop the render with an error if it encounters a missing texture map

parameters.label: Cancel Render if No Working GPU Devices are Discovered
parameters.label_norm: cancel render if no working gpu devices are discovered
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: Turning on this option will cause Karma to stop the render with an error if no working GPU devices are discovered. === Component Labels === (component_labels_tab)

parameters.label: Export Componetents
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: A space-separated list of shading component names that will be computed for export. If you have defined new component labels in your materials, these can be added to the list so that they are exported for per-component export planes. If you are not using some components, remove them from the list to improve render efficiency. PBR light exports assume that this list is complete - that is, all components created by shaders are listed. If there are unlisted components, light exports may be missing illumination from these components.

parameters.label: Diffuse Components
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: A space-separated list of component types that will behave like diffuse bounces. This will affect which reflection scope is used based on the ray type and also which bounce limit to use.  Uncategorized component types are assumed to be reflections.

parameters.label: Refract Components
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: A space-separated list of component types that will behave like refract bounces.  This will affect which reflection scope is used based on the ray type and also which bounce limit to use.  Uncategorized component types are assumed to be reflections.

parameters.label: Volume Components
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: A space-separated list of component types that will behave like volume bounces.  This will affect which reflection scope is used based on the ray type and also which bounce limit to use.  Uncategorized component types are assumed to be reflections.

parameters.label: SSS Components
parameters.heading: Secondary Samples
parameters.description: A space-separated list of component types that will behave like subsurface scatter bounces.  This will affect which reflection scope is used based on the ray type and also which bounce limit to use.  Uncategorized component types are assumed to be reflections.

floor.definition: summary AND >=1 documented parameter with a non-empty description  (I0-FLOOR, adopted verbatim)

deprecation.tier: VERIFIED-DOC + VERIFIED-RUNTIME (union, sides recorded separately — never collapsed to one boolean)

entries.title: Karma Render Settings
entries.summary: Configure Render Settings for Karma.

parameters.label: RenderSettings Primitive Path
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: This node creates a `RenderSettings` prim with the configuration you set up using the parameters. This is the scene tree path where this node will create the `RenderSettings` prim.

parameters.label: RenderProducts Parent Primitive Path
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: The location where the Render Products should be created.

parameters.label: RenderVar Parent Primitive Path
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: The location where the Render Vars should be created.

parameters.label: Output Picture
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: An output image filename (usually an `.EXR` file), or `ip` which renders the image in [MPlay|/mplay]. Include `$F` in the file name to insert the frame number. This is necessary when rendering animation. See [expressions in file names|/render/expressions] for more information.

parameters.label: Camera
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: Path to a USD camera (`UsdGeomCamera`) prim to render the scene from.

parameters.label: Resolution Mode
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: Use the USD Camera's aperture aspect ratio to automatically set one dimension of the resolution. The computed parm is set using an expression, but is locked to prevent accidental edits.

parameters.label: Resolution
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: The horizontal and vertical size of the output image, in pixels.

parameters.label: Engine Settings
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: Select the rendering engine.

parameters.label: Simplified Shading
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: Disable all shading and lighting (render with one headlight on the camera). This might be useful for preview purposes if a shaded view is too slow to render.

parameters.label: Primary Samples
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: When __Engine Settings__ is __CPU Parameters__, this is the number of ray-samples sent through each pixel. More samples will result in a less noisy image. Note that __Primary Samples__ and __Pixel Samples__ are the same.

parameters.label: Path Traced Samples
parameters.heading: Render Settings Prim
parameters.description: When __Engine Settings__ is __XPU Parameters__, this is the number of ray-samples sent through each pixel when using the path-traced convergence mode. More samples will result in a less noisy image. == Rendering == (rendering_tab)

parameters.label: TIP
parameters.heading: Secondary
parameters.description: For an in-depth explanation of primary and secondary samples, please take a look at the [Sampling|/solaris/kug/sampling] page of the Karma User Guide.

parameters.label: Min Secondary Samples
parameters.heading: Secondary
parameters.description: Minimum number of rays to cast in per-component variance anti-aliasing. The value, given here, is multiplied with the settings of the various __Indirect Samples Quality__ parameters for diffuse, reflection, volumes, etc.

parameters.label: Max Secondary Samples
parameters.heading: Secondary
parameters.description: Maximum number of rays to cast in per-component variance anti-aliasing. The value, given here, is multiplied with the settings of the various __Indirect Samples Quality__ parameters for diffuse, reflection, volumes, etc.

parameters.label: Diffuse Quality
parameters.heading: Indirect Samples Quality
parameters.description: This parameter acts as a multiplier on __Min Secondary Samples__ and __Max Secondary Samples__ for indirect diffuse component.

parameters.label: Reflection Quality
parameters.heading: Indirect Samples Quality
parameters.description: This parameter acts as a multiplier on __Min Secondary Samples__ and __Max Secondary Samples__ for indirect reflect component.

parameters.label: Refraction Quality
parameters.heading: Indirect Samples Quality
parameters.description: This parameter acts as a multiplier on __Min Secondary Samples__ and __Max Secondary Samples__ for indirect refract component.

parameters.label: Volume Quality
parameters.heading: Indirect Samples Quality
parameters.description: This parameter acts as a multiplier on __Min Secondary Samples__ and __Max Secondary Samples__ for indirect volume component.

parameters.label: SSS Quality
parameters.heading: Indirect Samples Quality
parameters.description: This parameter acts as a multiplier on __Min Secondary Samples__ and __Max Secondary Samples__ for the SSS component.

parameters.label: Light Sampling Mode
parameters.heading: Lights Quality
parameters.description: Whether Karma should perform uniform sampling of lights or whether rendering should use the light tree. The light tree can be significantly faster for scenes that have large numbers of lights.

parameters.label: Light Sampling Quality
parameters.heading: Lights Quality
parameters.description: This is a global control to improve sampling quality for all lights. This acts as a multiplier on the individual light quality controls. Increasing the quality will improve direct light sampling as well as shadows/occlusion.

parameters.label: Screendoor Samples
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: The number of transparent samples to be shaded as a ray travels through partially opaque objects. Increasing this value will result in less noise in partially opaque objects and is generally less costly than increasing __Primary Samples__, __Volume Step Rate__, or __Min|Max Secondary Samples__, This parameter will not have any effect on noise from indirect sources however. [Image:/images/render/mug/sampling/VolumeSamplingStochastic.jpg]

parameters.label: Volume Step Rate
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: How finely or coarsely a volume is sampled as a ray travels through it. Volumetric objects are made up of 3-dimensional structures called voxels, the value of this parameter represents the number of voxels a ray will travel through before performing another sample. The default value is `0.25`, which means that every one of every four voxels will be sampled. A value of `1` means that all voxels are sampled and a value of `2` means that all voxels are sampled twice. This means that the volume step rate value behaves in a similar way to pixel samples, acting as a multiplier on the total number of samples for volumetric objects. Keep in mind that increasing the volume step rate can dramatically increase render times, so it should only be adjusted when necessary. Also, while increasing the default from `0.25` can reduce volumetric noise, increasing the value beyond `1` will rarely see similar results. [Image:/images/render/mug/sampling_tab/VolumeQuality.jpg] === Limits === (limits_tab)

parameters.label: Diffuse Limit
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: Defines, how often diffuse rays can propagate through your scene. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/DiffuseLimit.jpg] Unlike __Reflect Limit__ and __Refract Limit__, this parameter will increase the overall amount of light in your scene and contribute to the majority of global illumination. With this parameter set to values greater than `0`, diffuse surfaces will accumulate light from other objects in addition to direct light sources. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/DiffuseLimitCompare.jpg] In this example, increasing the __Diffuse Limit__ has a dramatic effect on the appearance of the final image. To replicate realistic lighting conditions, it is often necessary to increase the __Diffuse Limit__. However, since the amount of light contribution usually decreases with each diffuse bounce, increasing the __Diffuse Limit__ beyond `4` hardly improves the visual fidelity of a scene. Additionally, increasing the __Diffuse Limit__ can dramatically increase noise levels and render times. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/DiffuseSubtleCompare.jpg]

parameters.label: Reflection Limit
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: The number of times a ray can be reflected in your scene. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/ReflectLimit.jpg] This example shows a classic "Hall of Mirrors" scenario with the subject placed between two mirrors. This effectively creates an infinite series of reflections. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/ReflectLimitCompare.jpg] From this camera angle the reflection limits are very obvious and have a large impact on the accuracy of the final image. However, in most cases the reflection limit will be more subtle, allowing you to reduce the number of reflections in your scene and optimize the time it takes to render them. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/ReflectSubtleCompare.jpg] Remember that the first time a light source is reflected in an object, it is considered a direct reflection. Therefore, even with __Reflect Limit__ set to `0`, you will still see specular reflections of light sources. This is a float because all limits are stochastically picked per-sample. For example, you can set the diffuse limit to `3.25` and have 25% of the rays with a diffuse limit of `4` and 75% of rays with a diffuse limit of `3`.

parameters.label: Refraction Limit
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: This parameter control the number of times a ray be refracted in your scene. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/RefractLimit.jpg] This example shows a simple scene with ten grids all in a row. By applying a refractive shader, we will be able see through the grids to an image of a sunset in the background. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/RefractLimitCompare.jpg] From this camera angle, in order for the image to be accurate, the refraction limit must match the number of grids that that are in the scene. However, most scenes will not have this number of refractive objects all in a row and so it is possible to reduce the refract limit without affecting the final image while also reducing the time it takes to render them. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/RefractSubtleCompare.jpg] Keep in mind that this __Refract Limit__ refers to the number of surfaces that the ray must travel through, not the number of objects. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/RefractLimitSurfaces.jpg] Remember that the first time a light source is refracted through a surface, it is considered a direct refraction. Therefore, even with __Refract Limit__ set to `0`, you will see refraction of light sources. However, since most objects in your scene will have at least two surfaces between it and the light source, direct refraction is often not evident in your final render. This is a float because all limits are stochastically picked per-sample. For example, you can set the diffuse limit to `3.25` and have 25% of the rays with a diffuse limit of `4` and 75% of rays with a diffuse limit of `3`.

parameters.label: Volume Limit
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: The number of times a volumetric ray can propagate through a scene. It functions in a similar fashion to the __Diffuse Limit__ parameter. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/VolumeLimit.jpg] Increasing the __Volume Limit__ parameter will result in much more realistic volumetric effects. This is especially noticeable in situations where only part of a volume is receiving direct lighting. Also, in order for a volumetric object to receive indirect light from other objects, the __Volume Limit__ parameter must be set above `0`. [Image:/images/render/mug/limits_tab/VolumeLimitCompare.jpg] With the __Volume Limit__ set to values greater than `0`, the fog volume takes on the characteristic light scattering you would expect from light traveling through a volume. However, as with the __Diffuse Limit__, the light contribution generally decreases with each bounced ray and therefore using values above `4` does not necessarily result in a noticeably more realistic image. Also, increasing the value of this parameter can dramatically increase the amount of time spent rendering volumetric images. This is a float because all limits are stochastically picked per-sample. For example, you can set the diffuse limit to `3.25` and have 25% of the rays with a diffuse limit of `4` and 75% of rays with a diffuse limit of `3`.

parameters.label: SSS Limit
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: The number of times a SSS ray can propagate through a scene. It functions in a similar fashion to the __Diffuse Limit__ parameter. This is a float because all limits are stochastically picked per-sample. For example, you can set the diffuse limit to `3.25` and have 25% of the rays with a diffuse limit of `4` and 75% of rays with a diffuse limit of `3`.

parameters.label: Color Limit
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: The maximum value a shading sample is allowed to contribute to an LPE image plane to reduce appearance of "fireflies" caused by undersampling of extremely bright light sources. Note that reducing this value can result in an overall reduction in the amount of light in your scene.

parameters.label: Shared Color Limit
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: When turned on, indirect bounces use the __Color Limit__ value and the __Indirect Color Limit__ parameter is ignored.

parameters.label: Indirect Color Limit
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: Color limit applied to indirect bounce only. Note that this parameter is ignored unless __Shared Color Limit__ is turned off.

parameters.label: Russian Roulette Cutoff Depth
parameters.heading: Volumes and Opacity
parameters.description: Depth at which indirect rays start to get stochastically pruned based on ray throughput.

parameters.label: Enable Depth of Field
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: Turn on the depth of field rendering. ~~~

parameters.label: Enable Motion Blur
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: Whether to turn on motion blur. Changing this in the display options will require a restart of the render.

parameters.label: Per-Object Motion Blur
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: Whether motion blur should be on or off for objects that don't explicitly have an opinion. If this is __On by Default__, the parameters below let you set the defaults.

parameters.label: Velocity Blur
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: This parameter lets you choose what type of _geometry velocity blur_ to do on an object, if any. Separate from _transform blur_ and _deformation blur_, you can render motion blur based on point movement, using attributes stored on the points that record change over time. You should use this type of blur if the number points in the geometry changes over time (for example, a particle simulation where points are born and die). If your geometry changes topology frame-to-frame, Karma will not be able to interpolate the geometry to correctly calculate Motion Blur. In these cases, motion blur can use a `velocities` and/or `accelerations` attribute which is consistent even while the underlying geometry is changing. The surface of a fluid simulation is a good example of this. In this case, and other types of simulation data, the solvers will automatically create the velocity attribute.

parameters.label: Motion Samples From Stage
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: For motion blur, karma gets the motion samples from the data authored on the stage.  Ideally, motion data should be authored at the shutter open and close times at a minimum.  For higher quality interpolation, additional samples can be specified between the shutter open and close times. Rather than having to specify the number of samples that karma should use, karma is able to find out how many motion samples are available and use those samples for motion blur.  If you specify the samples manually, Karma will interpolate the samples on the stage which may result in more (or sometimes less if undersampling) rendering memory, and can result in approximated motion. Please see the Karma User Guide for more detailed information.

parameters.label: Geometry Time Samples
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: The number of sub-frame samples to compute when rendering _deformation_ motion blur over the shutter open time. The default is 1 (sample only at the start of the shutter time), giving *no* deformation blur by default. If you want rapidly deforming geometry to blur properly, you must increase this value to 2 or more. Note that this value is limited by the number of sub-samples available in the USD file being rendered.  An exception to this is the `USDSkel` deformer. "Deformation" may refer to simple transformations at the geometry (SOP) level, or actual surface deformation, such as a character or object which changes shape rapidly over the course of a frame. [Image:/images/render/mug/blur/GeoTimeSamplesSimple.jpg] Objects whose deformations are quite complex within a single frame will require a higher number of Geo Time Samples.

parameters.label: Transform Time Samples
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: The number of samples to compute when rendering _transformation_ motion blur over the shutter open time.  The default is 2 samples (at the start and end of the shutter time), giving one blurred segment.

parameters.label: Motion Blur Style
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: Defines the type of motion blur. The default __Rotation Blur__ is suited for most applications, esp. spinning wheels or rotor blades, but also almost any other type of motion. __Linear Blur__ is only required in very rare cases.

parameters.label: Instance Velocity Blur
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: When defining motion blur on instances, the transform of each instance can be blurred in addition to any motion blur occurring on the prototype.  This option controls how the instance will compute the motion blur of the transform on each instance.  For example, when instancing prototypes to a particle system, you'd likely want to use velocity blur to compute motion blur (the transform on the prototype would be blurred by the velocity on the particles).

parameters.label: Instance Motion Samples
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: When motion blur on instances is computed using __Acceleration Blur__ or __Deformation Blur__, this parameter specifies the number of motion segments used for motion blur.

parameters.label: Volume Velocity Blur Scale
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: Velocity multiplier used to reduce or exaggerate amount of motion blur on volumes.

parameters.label: Instance Velocity Lattice Quality
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: Controls the resolution of the lattice super structure that is used for volume motion blur. Values closer to 1 result in a structure with velocities closer to the original velocity data but higher render time.

parameters.label: Enable Image Blur
parameters.heading: Camera Effects
parameters.description: If you turn this off, Karma still calculates velocities or motion vectors (and the velocities can be stored in an AOV), but it sends all camera rays at shutter open, so the image will not have any apparent motion blur. This may be useful if you simply don't want any motion blur to create a certain visual effect.

parameters.label: Disable Scene Materials (husk)
parameters.heading: Lighting Effects
parameters.description: When rendering in `husk`, disable scene materials.  You can also use the `husk` command line option `--disable-scene-materials`.

parameters.label: Disable Scene Lights (husk)
parameters.heading: Lighting Effects
parameters.description: When rendering in `husk`, disable all scene lights.  Emissive objects will still emit light. You can also use the `husk` command line option `--disable-scene-lights`.

parameters.label: Displacement Style
parameters.heading: Lighting Effects
parameters.description: This option sets the default displacement behavior for all objects in the scene.  It's possible that objects will override this setting.

parameters.label: Render Points as
parameters.heading: Geometry and Shading
parameters.description: When rendering point clouds, they can be rendered as camera oriented discs, spheres or discs oriented to the normal attribute.

parameters.label: Render Curves as
parameters.heading: Geometry and Shading
parameters.description: When rendering curves, they can be rendered as ribbons oriented to face the camera, rounded tubes or ribbons oriented to the normal attribute attached to the points. When choosing __USD Default Behaviour__, the curves will be rendered as oriented ribons if there's a normal attribute or rounded tubes if there's no attribute.

parameters.label: Override Curve Basis
parameters.heading: Geometry and Shading
parameters.description: USD supports __Curve Basis__ types that may not be supported directly in Houdini.  In some cases, you may want to override the Houdini curve basis. For example, if you have linear curves in Houdini, you may want to render them with a Bezier, B-Spline or Catmull-Rom basis.  This menu will force Karma to override the basis that's tied to the USD primitives. Note that the topology of the curves must match the target basis.  For example, when selecting any cubic curve basis, every curves must have at least 4 vertices.  For the Bezier basis, curves must have `4+3*N` vertices.

parameters.label: Cull Backfaces
parameters.heading: Geometry and Shading
parameters.description: If enabled, geometry that are facing away from the camera are not rendered.

parameters.label: Enable Caustics
parameters.heading: Enable Caustics
parameters.description: Allows evaluation of glossy BSDF that's seen by indirect diffuse bounce. This is a brute-force solution which may require significant number of diffuse rays to resolve, especially if __Caustics Roughness Clamp__ parameter is set to very small value or Indirect Guiding feature is disabled.

parameters.label: Caustics Roughness Clamp
parameters.heading: Enable Caustics
parameters.description: Increasing this value can make caustics less noisy at the cost of accuracy.

parameters.label: Ray Bias
parameters.heading: Shading
parameters.description: The minimum distance used when testing if _secondary rays_ from a surface intersect with other objects in the scene. The distance is measure from surface along the direction of the ray. Objects within the ray bias distance are ignored.

parameters.label: Constrain by Maximum Roughness
parameters.heading: Shading
parameters.description: Roughness parameter in GGX BSDFs are clamped by the maximum roughness value propagated down the ray chain in pathtracing. Enabling this option can cut out a lot of noise in indirect specular (in particular, cases where glossy surface is reflected by a rough specular surface) at the cost of a bit of accuracy.

parameters.label: Dicing Camera
parameters.heading: Dicing
parameters.description: Specifies a camera that is used for dicing complicated surfaces.  This can provide consistent dicing of surfaces when the viewing camera is moving.

parameters.label: Offscreen Quality
parameters.heading: Dicing
parameters.description: This parameter controls the shading quality scale factor for geometry that is not directly visible to the camera. For geometry that is outside the field of view (i.e. visible only to secondary rays), Karma will smoothly reduce the shading quality based on the angle between the geometry and the edge of the viewing frustum.  Smaller values can increase performance particularly in scenes where the camera is within the displacement bound of nearby geometry, where it permits the hidden primitives to be diced more coarsely than those that are directly visible.

parameters.label: Dicing Quality Scale
parameters.heading: Dicing
parameters.description: This parameter is a global multiplier for dicing quality of all objects.

The __Random__ method is mainly here for completeness and could give slightly better results with thick lines. * __Determined__ uses a fixed stencil sample pattern that creates a less noisy result. * __Random__ uses a variable stencil sample pattern that results in more noise.
